newsitem.title: USA: U.S. expects 78,000 refugees in next year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expects 78,000 refugees in next year.

text.p: The United States expects to admit about 78,000 refugees in the next 12 months, most of them from Bosnia and the former Soviet Union, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

The number is about 6,000 more than in the current U.S. fiscal year that ends on Monday, but 22,000 less than the previous year, Under Secretary of State Timothy Wirth told a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. He said the figures reflected changing world conditions.

Wirth said the United States had set a ceiling of 18,000 refugees from Bosnia from all ethnic groups in the next 12 months, 3,000 more than this year when only Bosnian Moslems with relatives in the United States were eligible for resettlement without U.N. referral.

He said other refugee ceilings for 1997 were 30,000 from the former Soviet Union, 10,000 from Indochina, 7,000 from Africa, 4,000 from Cuba and the rest of Latin America and 4,000 from the Near East and South Asia. The other slots will be held in reserve for use as needed.

Wirth said only about 100,000 of two million Bosnians who had been displaced by the war had returned to their homes. "We are committed to make the Dayton accords (which call for resettlement) work," he said.

Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum told reporters at the State Department that refugees were one of the main issues discussed on Thursday by Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Bosnian leaders at a meeting in Washington.

"Freedom of movement and refugee return is something which has been discussed a number of times, and which everyone agrees has not been moving as fast as it should and, again, we will be giving strong support to that," Kornblum said.
Wirth said 1997 would probably be the last year of large scale refugee processing in Southeast Asia, which began in 1975 after North Vietnam defeated South Vietnam.
More than 1.2 million Indochinese have been admitted to the United States under a programme to help those who were U.S. allies or who were children of American soldiers.

The United States admits refugees if they can show that they are likely to face persecution if they are forced to return to their home countries. The refugee programme is separate from aliens who are admitted as immigrants.

Senator Alan Simpson, Republican of Wyoming, urged the administration to limit refugee admissions to those who truly needed to be resettled on a case by case basis. He said the current programme was sometimes used to make political statements.
